title: Benchmarking machine learning across development reveals stage-specific neuroanatomical sex signatures.
summary: Machine learning (ML) offers powerful approaches for identifying multivariate patterns in neuroimaging data, yet the biological validity and interpretability of the discriminative patterns learned by such models remain incompletely understood. Here, we benchmarked multiple ML approaches for sex classification across development (8-21 years) on structural neuroimaging data and investigated the effects of age on model performance and feature stability. Linear and nonlinear models demonstrated comparable classification performance, indicating that high predictive accuracy can be achieved without relying on highly complex architectures; however, age-stratified analyses and cross-age generalization tests demonstrated that developmental stage influences classification performance, and consistency of learned neuroanatomical features. To assess biological interpretability, we applied SHAP and LIME explainability methods and developed a comprehensive framework for translating feature attributions into biologically interpretable patterns. Sex-discriminative regions were distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical structures and exhibited marked developmental variation. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of interpretable ML for developmental neuroimaging and highlight the importance of evaluating predictive performance while simultaneously taking biological validity, developmental specificity, and attribution stability into consideration.

title: Jump: Making Large-Scale Connectomics Accessible
summary: Large-scale connectomic resources generated from volumetric electron microscopy (EM) have transformed neuroscience by enabling detailed 3D reconstructions of cellular and subcellular morphology and connectivity across hundreds of thousands of cells in diverse tissues and organisms. Recent advances in machine learning-based cell classification and automated segmentation have enabled large-scale annotation of these datasets, yet barriers remain in validating automated classifications and extracting biological insights. To address these challenges, we developed Jump, a suite of user-friendly web-based platforms generated using Claude. These platforms support interactive exploration, expert-guided community review, and quantitative analysis of multiple publicly available EM datasets, while building a growing repository of community-generated annotations. Using uJump, which hosts data from the MICrONS mouse visual cortex dataset, as an example, we demonstrate rapid retrieval of specific cell populations, region-of-interest filtering, biological inspection of cells, and extraction of quantitative morphological and spatial metrics. We showcase analytical features including cell abundance and spatial organisation, connectivity, local cellular neighbourhoods, and volumetric measurements. Using pericytes and endothelial cells as a case study on the cortical vasculature, we further demonstrate how manual review and reclassification can generate accurately identified cell populations for downstream analyses. Consistent with the open-science principles underpinning many large-scale EM resources, Jump is designed to enable broad community participation. By lowering technical barriers to the use of EM datasets, Jump increases analytical efficiency and promotes collaborative efforts to accurately classify cells and structures. Expert-reviewed annotations can be shared across the community, allowing users to build on existing work rather than repeatedly validating the same automated classifications. Collectively, Jump will help researchers to accelerate biological discovery from connectomic datasets.

title: A machine learning framework for evolutionary model classification
summary: Machine learning algorithms are increasingly used across scientific disciplines, but remain absent from several areas of comparative biology. One example is evolutionary model selection, which typically relies on likelihood-based methods to identify the model among a candidate set that best explains trait evolution across a phylogeny. This approach requires all candidate models to have a tractable likelihood function yet this may not the case for complex models. Alternative likelihood-free inference methods are available but their application is limited in scalability and flexibility. Both classes of methods struggle with discriminating models that yield statistically similar patterns in trait data. Here, I introduce a machine learning framework to perform evolutionary model classification from comparative data. Using simulated datasets, I demonstrate that the approach improves model discriminability relative to conventional likelihood-based model fitting but does not overcome model non-identifiability. I then revisit an analysis of early burst signals in comparative data to assess how a machine learning approach alters the patterns of early burst support obtained through likelihood-based inference. Finally, I discuss future extensions of this framework and their potential to improve both our representation and understanding of evolutionary process-to-pattern mapping.

title: Role-Aware Line-Graph Neural Networks for Interpretable Prediction of Pairwise Microbial Interactions
summary: Predicting how microbial species affect each other's growth is a key challenge in microbial ecology. Using one of the largest available pairwise interaction datasets, comprising 20 soil bacteria co-cultured under 39 carbon conditions (15{,}074 directional measurements), we predicted whether one species has a positive or negative effect on the growth of another from monoculture growth, metabolic profiles, and phylogeny. Existing machine learning approaches treat each measurement as an independent sample, although experiments that share a species under the same condition are biologically related. We therefore represented the data as a role-aware line graph: each node is one directional measurement, and two nodes are connected when, under the same carbon condition, they share the same effector or the same affected species. This allows graph neural networks (GNNs) to pass information between related interactions. Our role-aware GAT-SAGE model achieved an F1-score of 81.38% for one-way prediction, outperforming the 73.79% previously reported for Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). For two-way interaction types (mutualism, competition, and parasitism), GAT-SAGE reached a macro F1-score of 60.34%. This exceeded the 55.71% of a neural network without graph structure but was below the 64.24% of XGBoost. Mutualism remained difficult to predict for all models. Layer-wise relevance propagation showed that one-way effects depend mainly on monoculture growth, whereas two-way interaction types depend more on the carbon environment. Encoding the dependency structure of interaction experiments thus adds information beyond the features of each measurement and provides interpretable insight into microbial interactions.

title: Does embedding impact classification performance ? A small sample perspective
summary: Deep learning (DL) methods can address many challenges posed by high-dimensional and sparse microbiome data. In this study we applied and compared deep (DNN) and shallow (SNN) feedforward neural networks combined with five dimensionality-reduction techniques: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), Autoencoder based Embeddings (AE), and convolutional layers (Conv). To establish baseline classification performance, the XGBoost was used, as it represents a robust machine learning based classifier with a relatively low number of hyperparameters. The task was to classify effective microorganism (EM) treatments based on intestine bacterial family abundance in common carp. In particular, the experiment involved 25 ponds that were divided into experimental groups. In each pond, the intestinal microbiome of five individuals was determined by sequencing two hypervariable regions of the gene encoding the 16s rRNA gene sequencing. The sequence reads were processed by QIIME2 and taxonomically annotated to the SILVA database, what resulted in 126 annotated families that were used as features in all downstream analyses. Abundance tables from 125 samples, transformed using the Centered Log-Ratio (CLR) method, were used to evaluate ten dimensionality-reduction and Deep learning configurations considering five-, three-, and two-classification scenarios. The DL models were optimized using cross-validation. To combat the overfitting that was present due to sparsity and small sample size, dropout and kernel regularization were implemented. During testing autoencoder embeddings achieved the highest classification accuracy (0.84), exceeding the XGBoost baseline (0.64), while embedding based on convolutional layers significantly reduced performance (0.44). PCA and SVD transformations showed comparable results (0.65), whereas NMF often failed to converge, likely due to incompatibility with CLR-transformed data. Best classification results were obtained for models that implemented AE embedding, it is most likely caused by their ability to capture non-linear patterns in the data. All models showed stable training behavior, with loss functions consistently decreasing across epochs. The SNN models were markedly less computationally intensive, than DNN. AE and NMF based embeddings were the most resource hungry (Wall Clock Time and RAM). Our results show (1): SNN architectures performed slightly worse than DNN, due to the fact of lesser informative capacity of the models. (2): Dimensionality reduction impacts model performance, though not always positively. (3) EM supplementation causes significant changes in microbiome that can be captured by DL architectures. Future work will include feature-importance analysis, integration of environmental and host metadata, exploration of larger datasets and more advanced architectures. As well as validation of model quality on simulated datasets. Overall, these results indicate that DNN architectures combined with AE embeddings have potential to be used as high accuracy classification tools. Those tools when combined with feature importance can help researchers to understand changes made by EM supplementation in a microbial community.

title: VMDance: An Efficient and Interactive Molecular Dynamics Clustering Plugin for VMD
summary: Clustering is the standard route from a molecular dynamics trajectory to a small set of interpretable conformational states, yet it is usually performed outside the molecular viewer, leaving cluster assignments to be exported, tracked, and mapped back onto the structures by hand. We present VMDance, an open-source plugin that brings the MDANCE family of $n$-ary similarity clustering methods into VMD. Through a graphical interface backed by a C++ implementation, it provides \kmeans{} NANI, HELM, eQual, and DIVINE clustering, together with PRIME representative-structure selection. These methods scale linearly with the number of frames and support deterministic initialization, so partitions can be reproduced exactly and recomputed interactively. Cluster assignments, quality metrics, and representative structures are linked to the loaded trajectory, keeping the analysis of conformational states alongside the structures themselves. VMDance is freely available at \url{https://github.com/diegoenry/vmd-mdance-plugin}

title: Insights into Ice-Growth Inhibition and Hydration Ordering by the Ca2+-Dependent Antifreeze Protein MaIBP_RIV
summary: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) inhibit ice growth by binding to specific ice surfaces, although the molecular basis of this activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the ice-growth inhibition mechanism of the calcium-dependent antifreeze protein MaIBP_RIV from Marinomonas arctica using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. MaIBP_RIV exhibits stable binding to the primary prism and basal ice planes through its ice-binding surface (IBS), effectively suppressing ice growth. IBS binding to the secondary prism plane is weaker and only temporarily inhibits growth. In contrast, the non-ice-binding surface (non-IBS) is repelled by the growing ice front. Our results also explain that Ca2+; stabilises the IBS and essential for ice-growth inhibition, while removing Ca2+; reduces IBS flatness, which significantly impairs its ice-growth activity. Experimentally characterised mutations on IBS residues (S44Y, G63D, N65Y, and D87Y) result in continuous ice growth, consistent with their reduced antifreeze activity. Hydration analysis of water molecules around IBS and non-IBS suggests that, by decreasing the temperature from 300K to 240K, the water molecules around IBS show more ice-like ordering compared to those around the non-IBS.

title: Structural deformations of lipid bilayers around membrane proteins inform oligomerization type
summary: A functional definition of a membrane protein's structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the polypeptide and the structure of the membrane around it. Biological membranes are composed of self-assembled lipid bilayers, with membrane proteins acting as inclusions that perturb this phase. These inclusions induce long-range changes in membrane structure and create an intrinsic, lipid-mediated driving force for membrane protein association. The question is how much different membrane protein folds shape their surrounding membrane to tune the affinity and specificity of this driving force. To investigate this, we conducted a computational study to evaluate whether different membrane protein oligomers exhibit characteristic membrane defects that indicate specificity in complexation. We performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric states of ten different channels and transporters in POPC bilayers and evaluated changes in membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameters. We found that all the proteins affect their surrounding membrane up to 3 nm from the protein surface. However, we observed larger defects at oligomeric interfaces for obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes, suggesting that their oligomerization is partly driven by burial of membrane defects. In contrast, oligomers that adopt different quaternary structures across homologs show weaker perturbations at known binding interfaces, and larger perturbations at lipid-facing surfaces. Nevertheless, all systems show fewer membrane defects upon oligomerization, suggesting an underlying lipid-mediated driving force that each protein fold modulates to tune affinity via membrane-mediated oligomerization.

title: Molpylot: a shared workspace for human-AI collaboration in molecular simulation
summary: Rigorous biomolecular simulation requires a long chain of physical decisions across fragmented tools. Language-model agents offer to automate this work, yet current agents operate outside the scientist's environment, generating ad hoc scripts or files that are effortless to launch but laborious to inspect and verify. Here we introduce Molpylot, an interactive modeling platform that unifies structure preparation, molecular dynamics, specialist protocols and replica-aware analysis in a graphical workspace designed to be immediate for the scientist, while exposing that same live session to any language model through 256 typed, tested tools. Operating within this shared workspace, the agent executes routine tasks under built-in safeguards that catch physical inconsistencies, while scientific judgment stays with the scientist. Across 18 systems, including asymmetric membranes, quantum-parameterized metal sites, enhanced sampling and free-energy calculations, we show how agents and built-in checks streamline setup, quality control and trajectory analysis. Molpylot is free for noncommercial use.

title: Beyond the Classical Flake-to-Vesicle Mechanism: Non-standard Vesicles Arise from S-Shaped Intermediates
summary: Vesicles are indispensable tools across numerous scientific and pharmaceutical fields, however, optimizing their properties necessitates a comprehensive understanding of their formation mechanism. The formation of lipid vesicles from bilayered lipid flakes has long been recognized as a fundamental step in vesicle preparation. The classical flake-to-vesicle mechanism, grounded in continuum models, describes this process as the transformation of a lipid flake into a regular spherical vesicle (RSV) via a cup-shaped intermediate. Nevertheless, this classical mechanism fails to account for emerging experimental observations of non-standard vesicles exhibiting diverse morphologies. Here, using extensive coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations combined with Markov state model analysis, we systematically revisit this transition process at near-atomic resolution. In addition to the standard product, we observe a notable fraction of non-standard vesicles, including small-sized spherical vesicles (SSVs), ellipsoidal vesicles (ELVs), and flake-derived vesicle complexes (FVCs). These non-standard products arise from S-shaped intermediates that differ from the classical cup-shaped intermediate, and the degree of S-shapedness is closely correlated with whether non-standard vesicles are generated and, if so, which specific types. This correlation holds consistently across four lipid systems with distinct compositions and transbilayer distributions. On this basis, we propose a generalized mechanism that explicitly incorporates the S-shaped intermediates and the non-standard vesicles. This new mechanism opens new opportunities for the innovative development of engineered vesicles with tailored morphologies for diagnostics, drug delivery, and therapeutics.

title: BMP-2 Release from Biomaterial Carriers: Reporting Heterogeneity and the Limits of Cross-Study Prediction
summary: Published release profiles offer a potential basis for predicting bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) delivery from biomaterial carriers, but heterogeneous reporting and study-specific effects complicate their reuse in machine learning (ML) models. As a preliminary exploration, we compiled 79 release experiments and 487 time points from 21 publications with a workflow that combined a large language model assistant and human verification, and we examined data comparability and cross-study prediction with ML models. Only 38 experiments (48%) reported BMP-2 alone as a percentage of the loaded dose. Within individual studies, binding components and coating layers were associated with slower release, consistent with established carrier mechanisms. Using carrier family as the sole predictor, a family-median model and gradient-boosted decision trees achieved lower mean absolute errors than a global-median baseline under random hold-out validation (0.42 and 0.44 versus 0.52 log10 units). Publication-grouped cross-validation did not establish a corresponding improvement (0.57 and 0.48 versus 0.50). Only 10 of the 28 modeling experiments belonged to carrier families represented in the training data under this scheme, and carrier family was strongly associated with publication. These findings highlight the need to distinguish within-study interpolation from cross-study generalization. Broader coverage of each carrier family, quantitative formulation and assay descriptors, and accessible numerical source data are needed to support predictive modeling of BMP-2 release.
